advances: A quantitative implication from affine hyperplane fractions to lattice covering radius, with a sharp rank-one calibration and a counterexample to replacing vanishing by a fixed sub-half fraction.

proof:
Choose $v_1,\ldots,v_r\in L$ greedily, each shortest outside the span of its predecessors, and write $\lambda_i=\lVert v_i\rVert$. These lengths are nondecreasing. At step $i$, any $i$ independent lattice vectors include one outside the preceding span, while the first $i$ greedy vectors have lengths at most $\lambda_i$. Thus the lengths are the successive minima. Use orthonormal coordinates adapted to the greedy flag and divide coordinate $i$ by $\lambda_i$ to form a linear map $D$. For a nonzero lattice vector with last nonzero flag coordinate $j$, its original norm is at least $\lambda_j$ and every nonzero coordinate is divided by at most $\lambda_j$. Thus the transformed lattice has no nonzero vector shorter than one. The open radius-$1/2$ ball injects into $\mathbb R^r/DL$ and gives
$$
\frac{\kappa_r}{2^r}\le\operatorname{covol}(DL)
=\frac{\operatorname{covol}(L)}{\prod_i\lambda_i}.
$$
The oriented determinant functional $x\mapsto\det(v_1,\ldots,v_{r-1},x)/\operatorname{covol}(L)$ is nonzero and integer-valued on $L$. Its dual vector has length at most $\prod_{i<r}\lambda_i/\operatorname{covol}(L)\le 2^r/(\kappa_r\lambda_r)$, also for $r=1$ with the empty product. Rounding coefficients in the basis $v_1,\ldots,v_r$ gives a point of their generated sublattice within $\sum_i\lambda_i/2\le r\lambda_r/2$ of every point of $\mathbb R^r$. Together these bounds prove the transference inequality. The inclusion $[-1/r,1/r]^r\subseteq B_2^r$ gives the bound on $C_r$.

For a shortest nonzero dual vector $w$, the values $w\cdot u$ on $a+L$ lie in a translate of $\mathbb Z$, and the projected ball has width $2R\lVert w\rVert$ in this functional. The support meets at most $2R\lVert w\rVert+1$ such levels. Each is an affine hyperplane carrying at most fraction $\xi$, so $1\le\xi(2R\lVert w\rVert+1)$. The projected support is a nonempty finite set, hence $\xi>0$ and the maximum is attained. Substitute the resulting lower bound on $\lVert w\rVert$ into transference. Under a block map the fine hyperplanes correspond via the invertible $A$ and every continuous section has the same multiplier $|\det C|$. Any covolume adjustment multiplies every section by the same additional factor. The fractions are unchanged.

For the rank-one calibration take $[0,2h]\times K$ with $h>0$, a compact convex $K$ of positive $s$-volume, and sample on $h\mathbb Z$. There are exactly three equal fibers at $0,h,2h$, and the endpoint fibers generate the whole hull. The base change $u'=u/h-1$ gives $R=1$, $\xi=1/3$ and $\rho=1/2$, which is equality since $C_1=1/2$. More generally, if a block image of the body contains a radius-$b$ ball, its fine width $2|A|h$ is at least $2b$. Its fine covering radius $|A|h/2$ is then at least $b/2$. This gives a fixed sub-half hyperplane fraction with persistent mesh under every uniformly round block normalization.

statement:
Let $L\subset\mathbb R^r$, $r\ge1$, be a full-rank lattice of Euclidean covering radius $\rho(L)$ and dual shortest nonzero length $\lambda_1(L^*)$. With $\kappa_r=|B_2^r|_r$ and $C_r=r2^{r-1}/\kappa_r$,
$$
\rho(L)\lambda_1(L^*)\le C_r\le r^{r+1}/2.
$$
Let a positive finite measure have fine base projection supported in $(a+L)\cap(q+RB_2^r)$ for some $q$ and $R>0$, and let $\xi<1$ be the maximum fraction of its mass on an affine fine-base hyperplane. Then
$$
\rho(L)\le \frac{2C_r R\xi}{1-\xi}.
$$
For a section law with $s$-volume on the continuous fibers and common weight per lattice base, an invertible block affine map with linear part $(u,x)\mapsto(Au,Bu+Cx)$ preserves these hyperplane fractions, including for $s=0$ with counting. Thus vanishing $\xi$ in uniformly bounded block frames forces the transformed radii to vanish. In dimension one the quantitative bound can be attained by an actual convex hull of its three equal sampled fibers.
title: Weighted affine hyperplane concentration bounds the Euclidean fine mesh
